---

### 1. Three is the right number — but not for the reason the comment gives (question 1)

I re-ran your experiment with the cutoff as a free variable, rewriting the served HTML at the proxy so `i < n` became `i < 0/1/2/3/6` without touching the repo. Throttled 1.6 Mbps / 150 ms / 4× CPU, median of 7, `/products/category/tents`:

| width | n=0 | n=1 | n=2 | **n=3 (shipped)** | n=6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 390 | 1540 | **736** | 744 | 748 | 840 |
| 834 | 2380 | **1404** | 1480 | 1488 | 1588 |
| 1440 | 2836 | 2972 | 1816 | **1788** | 1900 |

Your `i === 0` desktop regression reproduces independently (2836 → 2972). Summed regret against the best value at each width: n=1 = 1184 ms, **n=2 = 112 ms, n=3 = 96 ms**, n=6 = 400 ms. So 2 and 3 are statistically indistinguishable and 3 is very slightly ahead; 6 is worse at every width, which settles that branch with data.

**The stated rationale does not hold up.** The comment says "the second card … is what LCP reports". I measured the fractional boxes at 1440: cards are `397.328`, `397.328`, `397.344` — the **third** card is strictly the largest. Card 2 nonetheless won LCP in 35/35 throttled runs and every unthrottled run. So the reported element is not the largest and is not predictable from the markup; it falls out of paint/decode ordering across three same-size boxes. That is a *stronger* argument for your choice than the one written down: you prioritise the row because you cannot know which member of it will be reported, and betting wrong is a regression rather than a no-op. Worth rewriting the comment to say that, because the current wording invites the next person to "optimise" back down to `i === 1`.

Prefer 3 over 2 for the same reason: 3 is the only value that covers every card in the widest row, so it has no exposure to the case where card 3 starts winning. A responsive alternative (`<link rel=preload media=…>` hand-rolled, since `priority` cannot vary by viewport) would recover at most **84 ms at 834 and 12 ms at 390**. Not worth the machinery.

### 2. The `i < 3` cutoff falls in the middle of a visible row at tablet (question 2)

This is the visible cost, and it is at 834, not 390. At 834×1112 cards 3 and 4 sit side by side with **251 px of each above the fold**. Card 3 is `i=2` (eager); card 4 is `i=3` (lazy). Median load completion over 3 throttled runs:

```
834x1112   card#2 eager 1295 ms      card#3 lazy 3980 ms
```

A **2.7-second gap between two adjacent, equally-visible cards in the same row**. `shots/film-834-2200ms.png` shows it: three tents painted, and a bare grey box beside the third. At 1440 the equivalent band (cards 4–6, 63 px visible) is uniformly late, which reads as "more below" rather than broken — `shots/film-1440-2200ms.png`. At 390 there is no artifact; nothing below card 1 is on screen.

Nothing here is a correctness bug, and the fix is not obvious given the timing table — but the tablet artifact is the one real user-visible consequence of the choice, and it is not mentioned in the comment. Two options if you want it gone: extend to 4 at the `sm` range only, or accept it and note it.

**No layout shift.** CLS was `0.0000` in all 35 throttled runs across 3 widths and all 12 unthrottled viewport/density combinations. The `aspect-square` wrapper plus `width`/`height` reserve the box, so a late image paints into an already-correct slot. Your second sub-question is a clean pass.

### 3. On a phone the preloads beat the element they exist to help

Median completion at 390, throttled:

```
card#0 (LCP element, on screen) 797 ms
card#1 (off screen, top 946)    920 ms
card#2 (off screen, top 1432)   779 ms
```

Card 3 — which the user cannot see and will not see without scrolling — **finishes 18 ms before the element that defines LCP**. Three preloads share one pipe equally, so the LCP image gets a third of the bandwidth. That is the mechanism behind the phone cost; I measured it at ~12 ms rather than your 72 ms, but the direction agrees and the shape is the point.

### 4. The e2e guard cannot catch a revert of the decision it was written for

`LCP_VIEWPORT` pins `'category grid': 390`. That is the one width where the answer is trivially stable (card 1 is the only card above the fold). The desktop case — where `i === 0` costs **1184 ms** — is unasserted. I confirmed against the n=1 variant: at 390 the first image is still eager and still what LCP reports, so **changing `i < 3` back to `i === 0` leaves the new test green**. Given this repo's stated blind spot, that is the finding I would act on first. A second entry at 1440 asserting that *the LCP element is among the first three optimised images* (rather than "is the first") would cover it and would not be brittle against which of the three wins.

Two smaller notes on the same file:
- The generalisation from `img[alt="Our Mission"]` to "first optimised image" is safe — I verified `/about`'s first `<img>` is still `alt="Our Mission"`, so #157's coverage survives.
- I verified the `product detail` / 390 claim in the block comment (LCP is a `DIV`, 201300 px², vs the image at 133956). I did **not** verify the `/about` at 390 or home-grid claims in that comment; they were outside the changed journey.

### 5. `priority` in Next 16.2 does not set `fetchpriority`

Confirmed in the served HTML — the three `<img>` elements and the three `<link rel=preload as=image>` carry no `fetchpriority`. `apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/shared/lib/get-img-props.js:269,584` shows `priority` only flips `isLazy` and emits the preload. So the three preloads compete at equal priority, which is exactly why the row-wide fix works and the single-card fix does not. Also worth knowing before the next Image change: line 404 errors with *"has both `preload` and `priority` properties. Only `preload` should be used"* — `priority` looks soft-deprecated in 16.x.

### 6. Product detail: the preloaded image is entirely below the fold at 390

`shots/detail-phone-390-1x.png` — the description fills the whole viewport and the first gallery image starts at `top: 844`, i.e. exactly at the fold, not partially visible. The comment's "a small cost on phones" is right in magnitude but understates the shape: it is a whole off-screen preload, not a partial one. Fine as shipped (the 834/1440 gain is real and large), but the comment would be more useful if it said so.

### 7. Density holds up (question 4)

I verified the optimiser output by fetching it directly rather than trusting the DOM: `w=384 → 384²`, `640 → 640²`, `828 → 828²`, `1080 → 1024²` from 1024×1024 sources. Category card at 1440 2× needs 794 device px, requests `w=828`, gets 828 — clean. The detail image at 550 CSS px needs 1100 at 2×, requests `w=1080`, receives 1024, so **1.86× effective, 7% short of 2×** on the now-promoted LCP element. Pre-existing source-asset ceiling, not caused by this change, but this change is what makes that image the hero.

One trap for whoever reads a future `naturalWidth`: it reported 398 and 521 on these images, which looks exactly like upscaling. It is not — `naturalWidth` is density-corrected for `w`-descriptor srcsets (1024 ÷ (1080/550) = 521). Measure the optimiser's bytes, not the DOM.

### 8. Smaller items on the touched pages

- **Duplicate alt text.** All five detail-page gallery images carry `alt="TrailMaster X4 Tent"` — a screen reader hears the product name five times with nothing distinguishing. Adjacent to the changed line and now the LCP element. Pre-existing; worth an issue rather than a fix in this PR.
- **Price contrast is thin.** `p.text-gray-500` on the card = `rgb(106,114,130)` on `rgb(250,250,250)` = **4.63:1** against a 4.5 requirement at 18px/500. Passes, with almost no margin. Everything else is comfortable: h1 16.97, description 7.24, card h2 17.0.
- **Hover affordance has no keyboard equivalent.** `group-hover:opacity-75` on the card image has no `group-focus-visible:` counterpart, so keyboard users get only the UA ring.
- **Keyboard journey passes.** Tab order is Open menu → Sign In → Sign Up → cards in DOM order; the UA focus ring is present (`outline: auto 1px`) and not suppressed; Enter navigates; targets are 397×477 at desktop and 366×446 at 390.

### Checks not performed, with reasons

- **Loading / empty / error states:** the diff does not touch them. I did check the one interaction with the change — the `role="img"` no-image branch would silently reduce the preload count if it hit an index below 3 — but no product in any of the 7 categories has a null image, so I could not exercise it with real data.
- **Contrast on the detail page body copy:** the `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` sections inherit defaults untouched by this diff; I measured h1/h2 only (16.97 / 16.12).
- **The `/about` and home-grid entries in the new spec's comment:** outside the changed journey, stated above as unverified.</result>

`apps/web/src/app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` renders the gallery with `alt={product.name}` on every image:

```tsx
{product.images.map((image, i) => (
  <Image src={image} alt={product.name} ... />
))}
```

A product has three to six images. A screen reader announces "TrailMaster X4 Tent" five times in a row, with nothing to distinguish one from the next, and learns nothing about any of them.

The catalogue's own filenames suggest what they are — `main`, `angle`, `detail`, `lifestyle` — so the images are not interchangeable views even though the alt text says they are.

## Options

1. **Derive from the filename role.** `main.webp` → "TrailMaster X4 Tent", `angle.webp` → "TrailMaster X4 Tent, side view", and so on. Cheap, and better than what is there, but it invents a description from a filename rather than from the picture.
2. **Mark the gallery decorative after the first.** `alt=""` on indices 1+ keeps the first announcement and drops the repetition. Defensible if the images illustrate rather than inform — the product description carries the detail.
3. **Author real alt text per image**, which means data the catalogue does not currently hold.

(2) is the honest cheap fix; (1) reads better but asserts things about the pictures nobody has checked.

This is the same shape as #164 on the about page, where `alt="Our Mission"` duplicated the heading beside it. Both are cases where alt text was filled in from the nearest available string rather than from the image. Worth deciding them together.

The pattern in this PR is worth stating plainly: **my test has now been one-sided twice, in two different directions.**

First it asserted the LCP image was eager, but only at a viewport where the answer was trivially stable — so reverting the fix passed. `ui-review` caught that. Then, checking both viewports, it asserted the first N were eager but never that the rest were lazy — so prioritising *all 21 cards* passed every assertion. `verifier` caught that by actually making the change and watching nothing fail.

Both are the same underlying error: an assertion that only constrains one side of the thing it's protecting. Split out of #112. Deferred there deliberately, because the fix is a design decision rather than a bug fix, and both reviewing agents agreed it is real work worth tracking rather than folding in.

## Measured

At **390×844** with the chat panel open, a full Tab cycle has 43 focus stops. **26 of them land outside the widget on controls that are completely covered by the panel** — verified with `elementFromPoint` at each control's centre returning the chat panel, not the control. That is every product link on the home page.

The panel occupies 358 of 390px wide and 748 of 844px tall at that viewport. There is effectively nothing useful behind it to Tab to.

At **1440×900** the panel covers a corner and most focus stops remain visible. The asymmetry is the point: the panel *is* modal at phone width and genuinely is not at desktop width.

WCAG 2.2 **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)**, Level AA.

## Why #112 did not fix it

#112 gave the panel `role="dialog"` with an accessible name, focus-in on open, Escape to close, and focus return to the launcher — the four obligations of the ARIA non-modal dialog pattern. It deliberately did **not** add `aria-modal="true"` or a focus trap, and both reviewers confirmed that was the right call:

- `role="dialog"` is not a claim of containment; `aria-modal="true"` is. The panel currently asserts exactly the semantics it honours.
- A trap would prevent reaching the site navigation while the chat is open, which is wrong at desktop width where the panel occupies one corner.
- Dropping `role="dialog"` would lose the accessible name and the grouping boundary and would not move 2.4.11 at all — the controls are obscured by visual layering regardless of role.

## The fix, if taken

Modal **below `sm` only**, and all four parts together or none:

1. a scrim
2. `inert` on the page content
3. `aria-modal="true"`
4. a focus trap

Half of that is worse than none — `aria-modal` without a trap tells assistive technology something false, and a trap without `inert` leaves the obscured controls reachable by pointer.

## Worth deciding alongside

Whether the panel should become a full-screen sheet below `sm` rather than a floating card. At 390px it is already 358×748 inside a 390×844 viewport; committing to a sheet would make the modal semantics obviously correct rather than a judgement call, and would remove the 16px margins that currently serve no purpose at that size.

content.text:
Here's the decision, grounded in `chat.tsx:235-249`.

The panel is `fixed bottom-0 right-0` with `w-[min(650px,calc(100vw-2rem))]` and `h-[calc(100dvh-6rem)]`. At 390×844 that computes to **358×748** — 92% of the width, 89% of the height. Behind it there is nothing meaningfully reachable, which is why 26 of 43 focus stops land on fully covered controls. At 1440×900 the same rules put it in a corner and most of the page stays visible.

So the panel **is** modal at phone width and **is not** at desktop width, and it currently declares neither. #112 got the honest half right: `role="dialog"` without `aria-modal` claims no containment, so nothing lies — it just doesn't fix 2.4.11, because the obstruction is visual layering, not role.

**The decision is whether modality becomes responsive.** That's unusual — most dialogs are modal or not, full stop. Making it breakpoint-dependent means the same component honours different contracts at different widths, and the four parts (scrim, `inert`, `aria-modal="true"`, focus trap) have to switch together and live, including when someone rotates a phone or resizes with the panel open. Half-applied is worse than none: `aria-modal` without a trap tells assistive tech something false; a trap without `inert` leaves the covered controls clickable.

The second half is whether it also becomes a full-screen sheet below `sm`. That's not cosmetic — at 358×748 the 16px margins buy nothing, and a sheet makes the modal claim self-evidently true rather than a judgement call someone has to re-litigate. Keeping the floating card means shipping modal semantics for something that still *looks* dismissible-by-tapping-beside, which the scrim then has to sell.

questions.question: Should the chat panel's modality become responsive — modal below `sm`, non-modal at `sm` and up?

options.label: Modal below sm only (Recommended)
options.description: All four parts together — scrim, `inert` on page content, `aria-modal="true"`, focus trap — applied below `sm` and removed at `sm` and up, re-evaluated live on resize. Fixes 2.4.11 at 390 while keeping site nav reachable at desktop, where the panel really is a corner card.

options.label: Modal at every width
options.description: Simpler and unambiguous: one contract, no breakpoint logic, no resize handling. But it traps focus at 1440 where the panel covers one corner and the rest of the page is plainly usable — which is the thing #112's reviewers explicitly rejected.

options.label: Leave it non-modal, close #129
options.description: Accept the Level AA failure at phone width. The panel keeps semantics it fully honours, and no new behaviour ships. The 26 obscured focus stops at 390 remain.

questions.question: Below `sm`, should the panel become a full-screen sheet or stay a floating card?

options.label: Full-screen sheet below sm (Recommended)
options.description: Drop the 16px margins and rounded corners below `sm`; the panel fills the viewport. Makes the modal semantics obviously correct rather than a judgement call, and removes margins that serve no purpose at 358×748. A visible change to how the chat looks on phones.

options.label: Keep the floating card
options.description: Add only the modal parts; the panel keeps its margins and rounded corners at 390. Smaller visual diff, but ships modal semantics for something that still reads as a floating card with page visible around its edge — the scrim has to carry that alone.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/contoso
gh issue create --title "Chat panel entirely hides 4 focus stops at 1440 (WCAG 2.4.11), which #129 deliberately does not fix" --label bug --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
Found while implementing #129. Splitting it out rather than folding it in, because #129's design decision was explicitly *non-modal at `sm` and up* — so this is out of scope there by construction, not an oversight.

## Measured

At **1440×900** with the chat panel open, a Tab cycle visits 27 distinct focus stops. **4 of them are entirely hidden behind the chat panel** — every sampled point (centre and all four corners, inset 2%) returns the panel rather than the control:

- `TrailLite Daypack`
- `RainGuard Hiking Jacket`
- `TrekStar Hiking Sandals`
- `CompactCook Camping Stove`

Entirely hidden is the threshold that matters: WCAG 2.2 **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)**, Level AA, is failed only when the focused component is *completely* covered. (A further 12 stops are partly covered — not a Level AA failure, and not what this issue is about.)

The panel is 650×788 in a 1440×900 viewport — 45% of the width and 88% of the height, bottom-right. Calling it "a corner" undersells it.

## Why #129 does not fix this

#129 made the panel modal below `sm` only: sheet, `inert`, `aria-modal`, focus trap. At `sm` and up none of that applies, deliberately — a trap at desktop width would take the site navigation away while the chat is open, which both of #112's reviewers rejected.

So at 1440 focus still travels into the page behind the panel, and four product links are completely covered when it gets there.

`e2e/chat-modality.spec.ts` asserts the *desktop* case is non-modal, so it pins the behaviour that leaves this open. Its centre-point obscured metric is documented as stricter than 2.4.11 and is only asserted at 390.

## Options, none obviously right

1. **Scroll the focused element clear.** A `focusin` handler that scrolls a covered control out from under the panel. Fixes the criterion without changing modality, but fights the user's scroll position.
2. **Shrink the panel at desktop.** 650×788 is large for a corner card; less coverage means fewer hidden stops. Does not guarantee zero.
3. **Close the panel when focus leaves it.** Cheap and predictable, but discards the conversation view on an errant Tab.
4. **Accept it.** Level AA, four links, all reachable by closing the panel.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.
BODY
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

#129 is merged and closed via [PR #186](https://github.com/scottdensmore/contoso/pull/186).

## The decision you made, and what it cost

Modality is now responsive — the unusual part, since the same component honours different contracts at different widths and all four parts have to switch together and live.

| | below `sm` | `sm` and up |
|---|---|---|
| shape | full-screen sheet | 650×788 card (unchanged) |

I dropped the scrim the issue called for. Behind an opaque full-screen sheet it's invisible, and `inert` already blocks pointer and focus — it would have been four lines that do nothing.

## Two things measurement contradicted

**The focus trap doesn't provide containment.** I mutated it out and every containment assertion stayed green — `inert` is what does the work, since inert content leaves the tab order entirely. I kept the trap for Tab stepping into browser chrome and for degradation where `inert` is unsupported, and the comment now names which branches are tested and which aren't. Code review caught that an earlier version of that comment had gone stale the moment I added the wrap tests, and told a future maintainer the block was untested when it no longer was.

**The launcher was behind the sheet.** A `fixed` panel outranks a statically-positioned sibling in paint order regardless of source order, so the only way out of the sheet was underneath it. That showed up as exactly one obscured stop per 4-stop cycle.

Measured, and one of the issue's own options is dead: the hidden elements are **390–422px tall**, while the panel leaves only **12px above and 100px below**. No scroll position can ever clear them — option 1 in #183 can't work.

The more interesting result is what happens just above the current breakpoint:

| viewport | panel | % of viewport | entirely hidden |
|---|---|---|---|
| 390×844 | 390×844 (sheet) | 100% | **0** |
| 640×900 | 528×788 | **72%** | 5 |
| 768×1024 | 650×912 | **75%** | 4 |
| 834×1112 | 650×1000 | 70% | 4 |
| 1024×768 | 650×656 | 54% | 6 |
| 1440×900 | 650×788 | 40% | 4 |
| 1920×1080 | 650×968 | 30% | 4 |

At 640px — one pixel above where we just drew the modal line — the "corner card" covers 72% of the viewport. Calling that non-modal is the same mistake #129 fixed at 390, one breakpoint up.

questions.question: Where should the sheet/modal boundary sit?

options.label: Move to `lg` (1024px) (Recommended)
options.description: Sheet below 1024, card at 1024 and up. Justified by measurement: the card covers 70-75% of the viewport at 640, 768 and 834, which is not a corner. Fixes those three widths outright (0 hidden). Cost: a full-screen chat sheet on tablets and small laptops — 834×1112 and 1023×768 become edge-to-edge.

options.label: Move to `md` (768px)
options.description: Sheet below 768. Fixes only the 640 case; 768 (75%) and 834 (70%) keep failing, which are the two worst coverage figures in the table. Smaller visual change than lg, but leaves most of the problem.

options.label: Keep `sm` (640px)
options.description: Leave the boundary where #129 put it. Every width from 640 up keeps its hidden stops, including the 640-834 band where the card is 70-75% of the screen.

questions.question: At the widths that stay non-modal, how should the remaining hidden stops be handled?

options.label: Close the panel when focus leaves it (Recommended)
options.description: A non-modal dialog that dismisses on focus-out. The only option that reliably reaches zero, since nothing can be hidden behind a panel that is gone. The conversation survives — turns live in the reducer, so reopening restores the thread rather than starting over. Mouse users see no change.

options.label: Shrink the panel at desktop
options.description: Cap the height so it is genuinely a corner card. Reduces how much is covered but cannot reach zero: any link that still falls under the panel is still entirely hidden, and the count is driven by where the product grid lands, not by panel area (1280 already measures 0, 1440 measures 4).

options.label: Accept the residual and close #183
options.description: Document it as a known Level AA gap at the widths that stay non-modal. If you pick `lg` above, that is 4-6 stops at 1024 and up; the controls remain reachable by closing the panel first.

Split out of #183. The fix there closes the panel when **focus** leaves it, which satisfies WCAG 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured) because that criterion is about the focused control. It does nothing for a pointer user.

At `lg` and up, with the panel open, walking the home page in 80%-viewport scroll steps and counting links fully covered at some scroll position:

| viewport | links fully covered | card coverage |
|---|---|---|

The decision there was that the panel is non-modal at `lg` and up, deliberately, so the site navigation stays reachable. Closing on focus-out was chosen because it reaches zero for the criterion under test. Extending it to pointer users needs a separate decision, because the obvious mechanisms all have costs:

1. **Close on outside click.** Standard popover behaviour, and it makes the panel genuinely non-blocking. But a stray click anywhere on the page discards the open chat, and clicks on page background are common.
2. **A dismiss affordance that is not the close button** — click-outside on the scrim only, or a drag handle. Needs a scrim, which #129 deliberately does not have at these widths.
3. **Shrink the card** so it covers less. Reduces the count without reaching zero, and does not help at 1024 where the card is proportionally largest.
4. **Accept it.** The links are reachable by closing the panel first, which is one click.

#183 is merged and closed via [PR #189](https://github.com/scottdensmore/contoso/pull/189).

## What the measurement changed about the plan

The decision you took was justified by one number: at 640px — one pixel above where #129 drew the modal line — the "corner card" covered **72% of the viewport**. 75% at 768, 70% at 834. Those three widths were failing 2.4.11 exactly the way 390 was.

The sheet now runs to `lg`, and at `lg`+ the card leaves when focus does. **Zero entirely-hidden focused controls at all eight widths**, up from 4–6 at every desktop width.

I also killed one of the issue's own options with a measurement: the hidden elements are 390–422px tall and the panel leaves 12px above and 100px below, so no scroll position could ever clear them.

## Three regressions I introduced, caught in review

- **Shift+Tab was undone.** Closing on focus-out ran the focus-return effect, which dragged focus back to the launcher — one keystroke dismissed the panel, scrolled to the link reached, then took focus off it. WCAG 3.2.1, and since the widget is last in the document, Shift+Tab is the *only* way out.
- **103 characters per line at 1023.** The sheet grew to fill widths its contents were never tuned for.
- **The cap then inverted the bubbles** — the assistant's sat right of the shopper's own.

And a defect the change made reachable: closing on focus-out unmounts the panel's `role="log"` mid-request, so a reply arriving after you tab away was announced by nothing — which is precisely the flow a non-modal panel exists to enable.

## Two false greens of mine

Worth naming, because they're the same failure twice. An assertion of `not.toBe('BODY')` that the launcher satisfied — which is *why* it couldn't see the Shift+Tab bug it was written for. And a negative assertion that raced React's re-render, passing against a deliberately broken build; I only found it because a mutation "survived" and I instrumented instead of accepting it.

I also nearly shipped an ESLint failure: I read `$?` from a pipeline and got `tail`'s status, not ESLint's. The real error was `setState` in an effect body — fixed by writing the announcement where the reply lands instead.

## Verification

Build, `tsc`, ESLint clean (exit codes read directly). 126 vitest / 33 files, 42 Playwright, all 7 CI checks. Six mutations each turn exactly one named test red. Server torn down; travel-app untouched.

**Filed:** #187 (mouse users still can't reach 6–7 of 22 links at 1024/1440 — a bare-page click fires no `focusin`, so this is keyboard-only, as is the criterion) and #188 (the 1024 card is untitled and still 54.6%; icon buttons 36×36 vs Send's 44×44).

24 issues remain open. The chat cluster is now #184, #185, #187, #188; otherwise #162 (hero `h1` overflows at 320px) is the most visible user-facing defect left.

Found by `ui-review` on `fix/hero-band-grows-with-its-content` (#149). Pre-existing — confirmed identical with the old `h-80` and the new `min-h-80` — so filing rather than widening that PR.

## The overflow

At **320px** the hero `h1` overflows: `scrollWidth: 350` against a 296px content box, because the word "Company" is wider than the box. `text-7xl` is 72px at every width, from 320 to 1920.

Two reasons no check sees it:

1. `layout.spec.ts`'s sweep starts at 360. 320px is still a real width — iPhone SE 1st gen, and any browser at 200% zoom on a 640px viewport.
2. It is a *text* overflow with no element box past the edge. That is precisely the case the horizontal check's own comment says it exists to catch, so the check would find it if the width were in the list.

## The same cause has a second effect

Unscaled 72px type is why the copy wrapped to three lines and needed #149's fix at all. The band grows to accommodate it, which is correct, but it grows a long way: **616px at 390 wide**, against a 320px design intent. In landscape that is worse — at 844×390 the hero is 102% of the viewport and at 667×375 it is 113%, so the whole first screen is hero and you scroll to reach any content.

A responsive scale — something like `text-4xl sm:text-6xl lg:text-7xl` — would fix the 320px overflow, bring the phone band back toward its intended proportions, and make landscape fit. Worth checking the subhead (`text-2xl`) and body (`text-lg`) at the same time; they are also fixed.

## While in there

Found by `ui-review` during #162. Pre-existing widget behaviour, surfaced rather than caused by that change — shrinking the hero band brought the body copy above the fold in landscape, where the launcher sits.

## Measured

At **667×375** (landscape phone) on `/`, the chat launcher — fixed 40×40 at bottom-right — overlaps the hero body paragraph by **40×31px**, and clips the subhead by a further 40×1px.

Pixel-sampled contrast in the overlapping region: **1.1:1**. The launcher is a white disc (`bg-white rounded-full shadow-lg`) and the hero copy is `text-zinc-100`, so the occluded words are white on white. The rendered text reads "From c[am]p[i]ng to" with letters lost under the disc.

No overlap at any other viewport tested (320, 375, 390, 640, 768, 1024, 1440, 844×390).

## Why it is not a hero problem

The launcher is `position: fixed` with `z-10` and no awareness of what is beneath it. Any page whose content reaches the bottom-right corner at a short viewport has the same exposure; the home hero is just where it is currently visible. Landscape phones are the worst case because the viewport is short, so content that would otherwise be mid-page sits in the launcher's corner.

## Worth considering

#162 is merged and closed via [PR #193](https://github.com/scottdensmore/contoso/pull/193).

| viewport | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 320×568 | 672px, **118%** of viewport, **+30px overflow** | 468px, 82% |

## Three measurements moved it off the issue's proposed sizes

The issue suggested `text-4xl sm:text-6xl lg:text-7xl`, and I built that first. Review caught that **36px made the `h1` smaller than the category `h2` below it** — the brand name rendered smaller than "Tents", inverting the page's own outline. It also made the heading non-monotonic: one line at 639, two at 641, so widening the window made it taller.

And `lg:text-7xl` had 2.7% of slack at 1024 — 72px inks 973px in a 1000px box. Which side of that a visitor lands on depends on the font their machine resolves from the stack: Arial and Verdana fit, DejaVu Sans wraps. `7xl` now waits for `xl`, where the margin is 283px.

Shipped: `text-5xl sm:text-6xl xl:text-7xl`, with the body's two-thirds measure returning at `md` rather than `lg` — held to `lg` it ran 131 characters at 1023, the fraction doing no work exactly where the viewport had grown enough to need it.

## Two things I got wrong and corrected

My landscape guard was named "leaves room for something else on a short viewport" but only measured the band's height. The band starts 48px down because of the header, so at 667×375 its bottom edge is at 392 in a 375px viewport — **the test's name claimed something its measurement didn't support**. Renamed to what it measures, with the shortfall recorded.

Then, filing the residual, I attributed it to `min-h-80`. Review pushed back and I verified across nine landscape sizes: **800×360 — Galaxy S20 landscape — fails at 368px, 48px above the floor**. Padding is the lever, not the floor, and lowering `min-h-80` alone would have fixed none of the failing rows. #192 is corrected.

Each half of the change is mutation-caught: reverting the `h1` fails at 844×390, reverting the subhead and body fails at 667×375.

**Filed:** #190 (chat launcher paints over hero copy at 1.1:1 in landscape), #191 (body runs 95 chars at desktop), #192 (landscape residual), plus notes on #188 and #173.
